issues.legal_issue: An order dismissing an application for temporary injunction as outside the scope of the injunction rule is an order under that rule and is appealable.
material_facts: The applicants sought a temporary injunction in an application invoking the procedural rules governing temporary injunctions and the court’s inherent powers.
The trial court rejected the application on the ground that the threatened execution of an eviction order was not an injury covered by the injunction rule.
The appellate court declined to hear an appeal, reasoning that the trial court had acted under its inherent powers rather than under the injunction rule.
issues.conclusion: The trial court’s order was made under the temporary-injunction rule and was appealable; the lower courts erred in holding otherwise.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 104 and Order XLIII rule 1(r) of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appeal lies from an order under Order XXXIX rule 2. Where a court considers an application under that rule and rejects it because the asserted harm does not fall within the rule, it is deciding the application under the rule, not exercising inherent powers. An appellant may challenge the court’s interpretation of the rule, including its understanding of injury. The court referred to Hemant Kumar v. Ayodhya Prasad, AIR 1957 MB 95, and Abdul Hamid Khan v. Tridip Kumar Chanda, AIR 1953 Assam 104, as authorities followed by the trial court on the underlying sub-tenancy issue.

predicates.temporary_injunction_application: A party filed an application seeking a temporary injunction under the procedural rules governing such injunctions.
predicates.rejection_based_on_scope_of_injunction_r: The court rejected the application because it considered the alleged harm outside the scope of the injunction rule.

issues.definition: When a temporary-injunction application is rejected as outside the scope of the governing rule, the resulting order is appealable.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court should not interfere under its special-leave jurisdiction with the refusal of a temporary injunction where no prima facie case is established and the trial court’s discretionary decision is not arbitrary or capricious.
material_facts: The case reached the Supreme Court by special leave from decisions concerning the refusal of a temporary injunction.
The applicants’ application concerning their asserted status as tenants had been dismissed and that dismissal had not been challenged.
The opposing party had denied that a landlord-tenant relationship existed with the applicants.
The trial court found that the applicants had been guilty of delay and that the balance of convenience favored the opposing party.
The trial court concluded that the applicants had not established a prima facie case and had not exercised its discretion capriciously or arbitrarily.
issues.conclusion: Although the lower courts erred in holding that no appeal lay, the Supreme Court declined to interfere with the refusal of temporary relief because no prima facie case was made out and no basis for interference under Article 136 was shown; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: In exercising its jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court need not interfere with a discretionary order refusing temporary injunctive relief where the applicants have not established a prima facie case and the trial court’s discretion was not exercised capriciously or arbitrarily. The court also considered the unchallenged dismissal of the applicants’ application concerning their asserted tenancy, the denial of a landlord-tenant relationship, delay, and the balance of convenience.

predicates.no_prima_facie_case: The trial court found that the applicant had not established a prima facie case.

issues.definition: In a special-leave appeal from refusal of a temporary injunction, when the applicant lacks a prima facie case and the stated circumstances support the trial court’s non-arbitrary discretionary decision, the Supreme Court declines to interfere.
